Free Fares, Fuller Buses

Ridership, service and riders on Boston’s fare-free bus routes (23, 28 and 29)

Authors

Esha Gupta

Sahil Mittal

Published

October 2026

Abstract

In 2021–2022 the City of Boston made MBTA bus Routes 23, 28 and 29 fare-free. Using MBTA ridership, service and passenger-survey data together with U.S. Census data, we compare these routes with Route 22, which serves the same neighbourhoods but kept its fare. From 2019 to 2025 the fare-free routes lost far fewer riders than comparable routes, even though they lost service while Route 22 gained it. After adjusting for service, all three fare-free routes outperformed Route 22, and the advantage of 15–17 percentage points holds against the wider bus network. Route 29, whose service was cut by more than a third, shows the limit of the policy: free fares cannot make up for fewer buses.

1 Introduction

1.1 Research question

Who rides Boston’s fare-free bus routes, and how did ridership and service on these routes change over the years, compared with similar routes that kept regular fares?

1.2 Why this question?

For many city residents, public transit is the main way to reach jobs, school and health care, yet less than half the world’s urban population has convenient access to it (United Nations 2020). People without good transit face longer and less safe commutes (World Bank, n.d.), higher costs, and exclusion from economic and social opportunities (London School of Economics and Political Science, n.d.). Service that is frequent and reliable is what lets people depend on transit for daily needs (Institute for Transportation and Development Policy 2024).

1.3 Why Boston?

Boston’s rapid transit lines largely bypass Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan, which are lower-income neighbourhoods with mostly residents of colour, leaving them dependent on buses (Cook 2024). Boston’s fare-free bus program was designed to address this gap. Using federal pandemic relief funds, the City made Route 28 free as a pilot in August 2021, reimbursing the MBTA for each ride. After early results showed ridership gains and high rider satisfaction, the program expanded to Routes 23 and 29 in March 2022 (City of Boston 2026a). It has since been extended through December 31, 2026, with no decision yet on what comes next (City of Boston 2026b).

We compare the fare-free routes (23, 28, 29) with Route 22, which runs through the same neighbourhoods but still charges a fare.

2 Data

We combine seven public datasets (Table 1). Routes link across datasets through their MBTA route IDs, and neighbourhoods through census tract IDs.

Ridership comes from automatic passenger counters rather than fare data: riders on the fare-free routes do not tap a fare card, so fare data cannot count them, while passenger counters measure everyone who boards in the same way before and after the program.

3 Methods

3.1 Comparison design

We use a difference-in-differences comparison (Angrist and Pischke 2009): the change on the fare-free routes minus the change on a comparison route over the same period. This removes changes that affected every route, such as COVID and remote work, leaving the difference linked to free fares. The main comparison is Route 22; we check the result against the 8 busiest other routes (1, 66, 39, 57, 111, 32, 22 and 9) and all other routes. Silver Line routes are excluded because they are bus rapid transit with different ridership drivers.

3.2 Adjusting for service

A route that loses buses loses riders, regardless of the fare. Therefore, we also measure ridership relative to service, the change in riders per trip run:

\[ \text{Adjusted change} = \left(\frac{1 + \text{riders change}/100}{1 + \text{service change}/100} - 1\right) \times 100 \]

For example, Route 23’s riders rose 1.0% while its service fell 7.2%: 1.010 ÷ 0.928 = 1.088, so riders per trip rose 8.8%.

Periods: riders are compared from Fall 2019 to Fall 2025. Service data begins in 2020, so service is compared from January–February 2020 (before COVID and the program) to January–February 2025.

4 Findings

4.1 Who lives along the routes and who rides them

The three fare-free routes and Route 22 serve similar neighbourhoods (Table 2). Within a quarter mile of their stops, more than three-quarters of residents are people of colour, median household income is about $51,000–$57,000, around 4 in 10 households have no car, and more than half of renters are rent-burdened.

Their riders are also very similar (Table 3). Riders on all four routes are more likely to be people of colour and to live without a car than the average MBTA bus rider, and the fare-free routes’ riders are slightly less likely to be commuting to work.

Did free fares change who rides? Route 23 is the only fare-free route reported separately in both surveys. Compared with all bus riders in the same year (Table 4), Route 23’s riders remain more car-free and less likely to commute to work, and they remain more likely to be low-income and people of colour. The program kept serving the same kind of riders rather than attracting a different, better-off group.

Two cautions apply to Table 4. The MBTA’s definition of “low-income” changed between the surveys, so low-income shares should be compared within a year, not across years. And the fall in work trips happened on every route, reflecting the rise of remote work rather than the fare change.

4.2 Ridership on the fare-free routes

All four routes collapsed in 2020 (Figure 1). Route 28 rebounded sharply in its first fare-free fall (2021), and Route 23 climbed back to its pre-COVID level after becoming free in 2022. Route 22, which kept its fare, is still below its 2019 ridership. Route 29 stayed low, reflecting the service cuts described below.

4.3 Did ridership simply follow service?

If the fare-free routes had simply been given more buses, more riders would be expected regardless of the fare. Figure 2 shows the opposite.

Route 22 gained 2.9% more service but still lost 9.0% of its riders (Table 5). Route 23 lost 7.2% of its service yet gained riders, and Route 28 lost riders only in line with its service cut. Route 29’s ridership fell almost as far as its service: free fares could not offset deep service cuts.

Because Route 22 gained service while the fare-free routes lost it, the raw comparison understates the fare-free routes’ advantage. Once ridership is measured relative to service (Figure 3), all three fare-free routes outperformed Route 22: Route 23 by 20.4 percentage points, Route 28 by 11.4 and Route 29 by 3.6. Ridership usually falls less than one-for-one with service, so these adjusted gaps are an upper estimate; the true effect lies between the raw and adjusted values.

4.4 The fare-free routes in the wider network

Across the network, the fare-free routes recovered far more of their pre-COVID riders than other routes (Table 6).

The fare-free routes’ share of all weekday bus riders rose from 6.8% in 2019 to 8.8% in 2022–2023, before easing to 8.1% in 2025 (Figure 4). Much of the jump happened in 2020, before fares were removed, as riders on these routes kept riding through COVID more than riders elsewhere; the rise after 2021 (8.4% to 8.8%) is the part more plausibly linked to free fares.

The result does not depend on choosing Route 22 (Figure 5, Table 7). After adjusting for service, the fare-free routes did 15.4 to 16.7 points better than every comparison group, a remarkably consistent result.

Finally, Figure 6 shows how many more riders each route carries than its share of service would suggest. Route 23’s gap rose when it became fare-free (from +1.33 percentage points in 2021 to +1.85 in 2022) and stayed above its pre-program level, while Route 22’s gap stayed flat at about +0.6 to +0.85. Route 28, already fare-free in 2021, carries the most riders relative to its service of the four routes. Route 29 carries roughly its share of riders for its share of buses.

5 Limitations

Running list of data limitations and cleaning decisions, to be written up in the Quarto report. Add new items as they come up.

5.1 Study Design

  • Few treated routes. Only three routes are fare-free (23, 28, 29), so results show patterns rather than proof, and formal statistical tests have limited power.
  • Other changes overlapped with the program. COVID recovery, new bus lanes and the Bus Network Redesign happened in the same years. Comparison routes help separate these from the fare-free effect but cannot remove them entirely.
  • Route 29 is much smaller (about 2,100 weekday boardings in 2016 vs. about 12,000 on Routes 23 and 28). Combined totals mostly reflect Routes 23 and 28, and Route 29’s percentage changes can look large from small absolute changes.
  • No individual-level data. Rider and resident comparisons use aggregated survey and census figures, not the same people.

5.2 American Community Survey (ACS)

  • Boston only. Chelsea, Revere and Winthrop tracts (16xx, 17xx, 18xx) and non-residential tracts (98xx, 99xx) were removed. Neighborhood demographics are not available for bus routes outside Boston.
  • Tract boundaries changed in 2020. ACS 2015–2019 uses 2010 tracts (167 in Boston); ACS 2020–2024 uses 2020 tracts (191 in Boston). Only 147 tract IDs appear in both, so comparisons are made across route areas, not individual tracts.
  • Missing and capped income. In 2020–2024, median household income was missing (Census code -666666666) for 3 Boston tracts; two residential tracts were kept with income set to missing. Two tracts are top-coded at $250,001 (“$250,000 or more”).
  • Zero-population tract removed. One 2020–2024 tract (061202) had no residents and was dropped.
  • Tract averages are unweighted. Summary statistics average tracts equally regardless of population, so they differ slightly from citywide figures.
  • Estimates carry sampling error. ACS 5-year values are survey estimates pooled over five years, each with a margin of error.
  • Work from home changed commuting. Transit commuting fell from about 33% (2015–2019) to about 23% (2020–2024) of workers, largely because of remote work, which also lowered bus ridership system-wide.

5.3 Bus Ridership

  • Fall only. Ridership data covers one season (Fall) per year, so it shows year-to-year trends but not month-to-month changes.
  • Passenger counter averages. Values are averages from automatic passenger counters across sampled trips, not complete counts.
  • File formats changed over time. 2024 moved the year into a separate column and renamed sample_size to sample_count; 2025 used entirely different column names and short day-type labels (wkdy, sat, sun). All were standardized during cleaning.
  • 2025 weekday is a weighted average. The 2025 data reports Monday–Thursday and Friday separately. They were combined as (4 × Mon–Thu + 1 × Friday) / 5 to match the five-day weekday average of earlier years.
  • 2025 dip may partly reflect the format change. Route 28 weekday boardings were about 9% lower in 2025 than in 2024; part of this may come from the new data format rather than a real change.
  • 2020 is a COVID year. Fall 2020 ridership was far below normal and is excluded from before/after comparisons.
  • Fewer stops over time. The number of stop records declines from 2018 onward, reflecting stop consolidation and route changes.
  • Stop names may vary across years, so stop-level comparisons should match on stop_id.
  • Silver Line kept. Silver Line routes (741, 742, 743, 746, 749, 751) are bus rapid transit but remain in the comparison group.

5.4 Bus Arrival/Departure (Service Performance)

  • Data begins in 2020. The “before” period for service measures falls during COVID, when traffic and ridership were unusually low.
  • 2020 files differ. 2020 comes in four quarterly files; October–December uses different column names. About 20% of October–December 2020 trips could not be matched from start to end point, so trip counts for that quarter understate actual service. Median trip times, lateness and bunching remain consistent with earlier months.
  • Time zones differ by year. 2020 times are in Boston local time; 2021–2025 times are in UTC and were converted.
  • Daylight saving approximated by month. The peak-hour label treats April–October as daylight time. The actual switches happen in mid-March and early November, so the peak label is off by an hour for a few weeks each year. Lateness, trip time and bunching are not affected.
  • Missing trip IDs. About 8% of 2025 records have no half_trip_id and are excluded from trip-time calculations (but included in lateness and bunching).
  • Impossible trip times removed. Trip times below 0 or above 300 minutes (recording errors) were dropped.
  • Bunching calculated from our own gaps. The MBTA’s headway and scheduled_headway fields were mostly blank (and absent for frequent “headway” routes such as Route 28), so gaps between buses were computed from scheduled and actual times. A bus counts as bunched if its actual gap is under half its scheduled gap; buses that passed each other also count as bunched.
  • Peak definition. Peak = weekdays, 7–9 AM and 4–7 PM Boston time.
  • No dwell time. Data is recorded only at timepoints, so time spent boarding at individual stops cannot be measured directly; boarding speed is tested indirectly through trip time.
  • Early buses in fall 2020. Buses ran several minutes early from September 2020 onward, likely because schedules included extra time while traffic was light. Treated as a real 2020 pattern, not a data error.

5.5 Passenger Surveys

  • Route grouping differs between surveys. 2015–17 reports Routes 22 and 29 together (“22 and 29”); 2025 reports Routes 28 and 29 together (“28 & 29”). Route 23 is the only fare-free route reported separately in both.
  • 2025 release pools 2022–2025 responses, so it describes riders across the program period rather than a single year.
  • Income measured differently. 2015–17 uses dollar brackets; 2025 uses shares of Area Median Income. Low-income and minority classifications are the most comparable measures.
  • Sampling error. Both surveys are weighted samples; 2015–17 reports response counts but no margins of error.
  • Some 2025 income labels overlap as published (for example, “Less than 40%” and “30% to 60%” of Area Median Income).

6 Conclusion

Free fares did not reverse the post-pandemic fall in bus ridership in Boston, but they made a clear difference to how much of it the fare-free routes recovered. From 2019 to 2025, Routes 23, 28 and 29 together lost 6.3% of their weekday riders, against 18.7% on the busiest other routes and 22.8% across the rest of the network. This was not because they received more buses: Route 22, which kept its fare, gained service but lost riders, while the fare-free routes lost service and still held on to theirs. Once service changes are taken into account, all three fare-free routes outperformed Route 22, and the advantage of roughly 15–17 percentage points is consistent across every comparison group.

The program also kept serving the riders it was designed for: people in lower-income, transit-dependent neighbourhoods, most of them people of colour and many without a car. Route 29 shows the limit of the policy. Its service was cut by more than a third and its ridership fell almost as much, so free fares cannot substitute for frequent, reliable service. As the City decides what happens after December 2026, the evidence suggests that removing fares helps routes hold on to riders, but only alongside maintaining the service those riders depend on.

Use of AI tools

We used Claude, an AI assistant developed by Anthropic (Anthropic 2026), for support with Python code, debugging, chart design and editing text. All analysis decisions, interpretation and final writing are our own, and every result was checked against the data.
